name: Aortic dissection

matching.reasoningTemplate: Severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, especially with hypertension, raises aortic dissection.

redFlags: Tearing chest/back pain with pulse/BP differential — emergency imaging

clinicalPearls: Pain characteristically migrates as the dissection propagates, often shifting to the interscapular region of the back (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Systemic hypertension coexists in about 70% of patients with aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.2168).
Peak incidence is in the sixth and seventh decades, with men affected about twice as often as women (Harrison 22e p.2169).

A normal ECG showing no ischemia helps distinguish dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain, though dissection can rarely involve a coronary ostium and cause an actual MI (Harrison 22e p.2169).

On chest x-ray, ascending dissection often produces a widened superior mediastinum; a pleural effusion (usually left-sided) may appear and is typically serosanguineous rather than a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Although 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain is classic, acute aortic emergencies also commonly present with knifelike pain (Harrison 22e p.106).
Stanford type A or B classification is more practical for management than DeBakey, because DeBakey types I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).
harrison.pathophysiology: Dissection begins with a tear of the intima, most often along the high-shear right lateral wall of the ascending aorta or in the descending thoracic aorta just below the ligamentum arteriosum. Pulsatile flow dissects along the elastic lamellar plates of the media to create a false lumen; the initiating event may be a primary intimal tear with secondary dissection into the media, or a medial hemorrhage that secondarily disrupts the intima. The dissection usually propagates distally (sometimes proximally), may be limited distally by atherosclerotic plaque, and can re-enter the true lumen through a secondary distal intimal disruption. Underlying medial degeneration and conditions that raise aortic wall stress predispose to dissection. Two related radiologic/pathologic variants are intramural hematoma (rupture of vasa vasorum bleeding into the wall, without an intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (plaque erosion into the media); both can progress to dissection and rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168-2169).
additionalDifferentials: Acute myocardial infarction / acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, and dissection can occlude a coronary ostium) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Esophageal pain / spasm, which can mimic angina (Harrison 22e p.106)
nonInfectiousMimics: Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168)
Acute intramural hematoma of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168)
additionalInvestigations: CT (with contrast) — most commonly used given proximity of scanners to emergency rooms and rapidity; sensitivity and specificity >90% for the intimal flap and extent (Harrison 22e p.2169)
MRI — highly accurate for intimal flap, extent, intramural hemorrhage and penetrating ulcers; sensitivity and specificity >90% (Harrison 22e p.2169)

Transesophageal echocardiography — ~98% sensitivity and ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection (but not the arch); also assesses aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Transthoracic echocardiography — rapid bedside test, overall sensitivity 60-85% (>80% for proximal ascending dissection), less useful for arch and descending aorta (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Chest x-ray — may show widened superior mediastinum and/or pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169)
ECG — to look for ischemia and help differentiate from MI (Harrison 22e p.2169)
redFlags: Sudden, very severe tearing chest or interscapular back pain with diaphoresis, especially when it migrates (Harrison 22e p.2169)

New aortic regurgitation murmur (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur along the right sternal border) in a patient with chest pain — common (>50%) in proximal dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Pulse deficit or loss of pulses (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Hypotension with hemopericardium / cardiac tamponade signs (suggests retrograde type A dissection) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Acute neurologic deficit — hemiplegia/hemianesthesia (carotid involvement) or paraplegia (spinal cord ischemia) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Falling hematocrit with hypotension and pleural effusion (suggests rupture) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
harrison.prognosis: In-hospital mortality after surgical treatment of dissection is reported at about 15-25%; for medically treated uncomplicated type B dissection it is about 12%. Major perioperative causes of death and morbidity include myocardial infarction, paraplegia, renal failure, tamponade, hemorrhage, and sepsis. With careful follow-up the long-term outlook after discharge is generally good, with roughly 60% 10-year survival; patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for post-dissection complications (Harrison 22e p.2170).
pitfalls: Aortic dissection is a classic disease that is misdiagnosed as acute myocardial infarction — a dangerous error because anticoagulant/thrombolytic therapy for presumed MI can be catastrophic (Harrison 22e p.102, p.2169).
A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and does not by itself indicate rupture unless there is accompanying hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Transthoracic echocardiography is insensitive for arch and descending dissections, so a negative TTE does not exclude dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169).
harrison.severityClassification: Stanford classification: type A involves the ascending aorta (proximal dissection) regardless of tear site or distal extension; type B is limited to the arch and/or descending aorta (distal dissection). DeBakey classification: type I — intimal tear in ascending aorta with propagation to arch, descending and possibly abdominal aorta; type II — limited to the ascending aorta; type III — tear in the descending aorta with distal propagation. Stanford A/B is more practical for management since DeBakey I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).
